title: honor, not worship
hookLine: "isn't praying to Mary idolatry?" — the answer is one difference

lines: A WOMAN IN BLUE. A MAN WITH KEYS.
cards: Sooner or later a friend asks it, usually kindly: why do Catholics pray to Mary? Isn't that worshiping a statue? Walk into an old church and you can see why they'd wonder.
Plaster figures in niches. Faces in stained glass. Candles flickering in front of a woman in blue and a man holding keys.
Plenty of people raised Catholic were never given the answer either. It turns on one difference, and it's a difference people already live by.

teach.b: Catholics draw a sharp line between worship and honor. Worship belongs to God alone. Honor can be given to people: the way you'd honor a grandmother, a teacher, a hero.
Mary, the mother of Jesus, gets the highest honor of any saint, but still honor, not worship.
So why pray to them? Because what Catholics are doing is asking: pray for me. It's what you'd ask a friend.

Catholics believe in what the old creed calls the communion of saints: everyone who belongs to Christ, living and dead, is one family, and the family can still pray for each other. Death doesn't end the friendship.
So a statue works like a family photo. Nobody is praying to the plaster. And the saints were never perfect.

The man with the keys is Peter, who said three times, the night Jesus was arrested, that he didn't know him, then went out and wept. Catholics count him the first pope. A saint isn't someone who never fell.
It's someone who kept getting up. Other Christians see it differently: many Protestants honor the saints as examples, and don't ask for their prayers.

how: Catholics honor Mary and the saints, ask for their prayers, and keep their feast days through the year and on All Saints' Day, November 1; worship is given to God alone.

games.q: who gets what — tap the pairs.
p: given to Mary and the saints
said no three times, then wept

s: Catholics honor Mary and ask for her prayers; worship, in Catholic teaching, belongs to God alone.
in Catholic belief, the saints can still pray for the living
the communion of saints: one family, living and dead, praying for each other.
saints are people who never did anything wrong
Peter denied Jesus three times. saints fell, and kept getting up.

games.q: you're Peter, warming your hands by a fire the night Jesus is arrested. a servant girl asks if you know him. what does Peter do?
o: says yes, and is arrested too.
games.why: three times he says he doesn't know him. then the rooster crows, and he weeps. Catholics count him the first pope.

games.q: put the creed's phrase back together.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. Think of someone, alive or gone, who failed at something and kept going. On the first breath, picture their face.
On the second, remember what they got wrong. On the third, remember that they kept going.

wordCard.voice: The saints. Holy ones: honored, not worshiped, and still one family with the living. Fifth word.

orig.note: Latin: holy. the root of the word saint.

carryVoice: Your line: the company you're in. Flawed people, still going, still in the family. See you tomorrow.
